summary.text: 茶 names the tea plant and its prepared drink. Its written history is linked to 荼, whose plant-category element 艸 and sound element 余 form a supported analysis of that earlier graph.

formation.text: 茶 is a later graphic form linked to 荼. The earlier graph 荼 is analyzed as a compound: 艸 marks the plant category, while 余 supplies a sound cue. This analysis does not assign a separate meaning to every stroke in 茶.

components.text: In 荼, 艸 marks the plant category. This role belongs to the earlier graph and does not make every stroke of 茶 a separate meaningful component.
In 荼, 余 is analyzed as its sound element. In Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese reconstruction, its reading is compatible with 茶’s; this comparison does not identify 余’s original referent.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese reconstruction, 余 *la is compatible with 茶 *rlaː. Their modern Mandarin readings, yú and chá, differ.

history.text: The curated image shows 荼 in a modern rendering of the seal-script style associated with the Shuowen account. It illustrates the earlier graph linked to 茶; it is not a dated artifact.
茶 is described as a later form related to 荼. Medieval spellings vary, and accounts differ on when 茶 became a distinct graph; proposed Han forms and readings are also disputed or qualified.

uncertainties.text: The precise graphic path and date at which 茶 became distinct remain unsettled. Han uses of 荼 are disputed as evidence for tea; an older Shijing use refers to a bitter plant, though its exact species is uncertain.

The spoken word’s deeper origin has competing proposals: borrowing from Loloish or Austroasiatic sources, or development from 荼 ‘bitter plant’. These proposals concern the spoken word rather than the graph, and the source language and pathway remain unresolved.

senses.period: Tang period attested; earlier date unresolved
senses.text: 茶 is recorded for the tea plant. A Tang text describes tea as a fine southern tree, but the earliest date of this sense is unsettled.
Tang-period sources use 茶 for prepared tea. Proposed Han references written with 荼 remain disputed as evidence for this sense.

senses.gloss: infusion made from ingredients other than tea leaves
senses.text: 茶 is also recorded for brewed drinks made with other ingredients; the start of this use is undated.
A Ming example uses 茶 as a verb meaning ‘drink’; how this use developed from the noun is not established.
茶 is recorded as a metonym for betrothal gifts associated with tea; when this use began is undated.
茶 commonly names tea, including the plant and its prepared drink.

limitations.text: The Han 荼 passages are candidates, not uncontested evidence for an early tea sense. The listed senses do not identify the earliest historical use.

Phonosemantic compound. 艹 represents the meaning and 余 represents the sound.

Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *rlaː): semantic 艹 + phonetic 余 (OC *la).
茶, then slightly modified into a more conservative 茶, originates as a graphical modification of archaic 荼 (*rlaː, “bitter plant”), used for “tea” in classical sources. The modern version is unrelated to the bottom component of 條.
As tea may have originated from Sichuan, where the native Yi people speak Loloish languages, Sagart (1999) suggests that the Old Chinese item was possibly originally borrowed from Proto-Loloish *la¹ (“tea”), from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *s-la (“leaf; tea”). Schuessler (2007) traces its ultimate origin to Proto-Austroasiatic *slaʔ (“leaf”) (in Sidwell's 2024 reconstruction).
Alternatively, Qiu (1988) suggests that it might be a semantic extension of 荼 (*rlaː, “bitter plant”).

evidence.text: The entry is for 荼, not the later graph 茶: it glosses it as 苦荼 and analyzes it as 艸 (plant category) plus 余 as phonetic. This supports a phonetic role for 余 in 荼; it does not establish that every stroke in the later 茶 is a meaningful component.

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database describes 茶 as a later graph, written earlier with 艸 and phonetic 余 as 荼. It gives 茶 as tea plant and tea drink, and cites Lu Yu’s Tang-period 茶經, which calls tea a fine southern tree. It also records later uses for other brewed drinks and, in Ming usage, as a verb ‘drink’. These glosses do not by themselves date each semantic extension.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：茶

evidence.source: Zhang Yongmei, Essays on Linguistics (Peking University Journals)
evidence.text: The 2025 abstract argues that in the Shijing period only 荼 occurred and it did not mean tea; it assigns 荼 a tea sense and reading *deɑ by the Western Han at the latest, with 茶 appearing as a graphic derivative used alongside 荼 for tea. It argues the distinction developed gradually: Tang Buddhist texts show the tea reading of 荼 fading, 茶 increasingly replaced 荼 after mid-Tang, and later Ming dictionaries completed the separation. This is a recent scholarly account, not settled primary evidence; the page provides only an abstract.
evidence.title: “荼”与“茶”表茗茶的形音义源流试探

evidence.text: Mair argues medieval manuscript forms vary in their lower strokes and that 茶 was not necessarily an independent replacement of 荼 at first. In his account, surviving Qieyun manuscript evidence around 700 CE generally writes the tea plant with a graph transcribed as 荼; a 706 CE manuscript gives no 茶 form in its cited line, while a reading that mentions 茶 in another manuscript requires image verification. He reports Guangyun (1007 CE) lists 茶 as俗 relative to the regular form. He also cautions that a Han tomb seal often read 茶陵 may instead read 荼陵. This challenges simple claims that 茶 was securely established in Han times or invented by Lu Yu.
evidence.title: Sinographs for “tea”

This is a Middle Chinese system/classification, distinct from the Old Chinese reconstructions in the dossier. It supports comparison with a historical reading of the whole character but the page does not independently supply a matching reconstructed pronunciation for 余.

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.

gaps: No glyph image was visually inspected; graph-shape descriptions are attributed to textual sources only.
No inspected primary manuscript image establishes the earliest date when 茶 became a distinct spelling; the manuscript discussion is secondary and reports variation and transcription uncertainty.
The Han 僮約 use of 荼 is disputed as an attestation of tea; the exact referent of Shijing 荼 is also uncertain.
The early graph 荼 has an explicit 余 phonetic analysis, and Zhengzhang’s listed Old Chinese values are compatible, but this pass did not inspect a primary Old Chinese reconstruction source for 余.

The Loloish/Sino-Tibetan and Austroasiatic word-origin proposals remain competing reports. Evidence inspected here does not independently verify the donor forms, donor chronology, or borrowing direction.
No basis was found to claim 茶 is a whole-graph phonetic loan; proposed loan theories concern the spoken word for tea, independently of the graph’s component analysis.
The inspected Shuowen.cn page did not expose the relevant entry text. The dossier’s Shuowen quotation is treated as supplied evidence, not freshly verified here.
No primary manuscript image was inspected to establish the earliest date of an independent 茶 graph; existing source reports differ over early Han forms and their readings.
The Shijing 荼 bitter-plant use is an older textual use, but exact botanical identification and its semantic relation to tea remain unsettled. The Han 僮約 荼 forms are disputed as tea attestations.

No donor-language primary dictionary or specialist source was inspected to independently validate Proto-Loloish *la¹, Proto-Sino-Tibetan *s-la, or Proto-Austroasiatic *slaʔ, their chronology, or the loan direction. The name/pronunciation of any depicted object is not implicated: no whole-graph loan claim is supported.

items.period: Shuowen seal-script style; the represented form is not independently dated by this modern vector file
items.tradition: Chinese seal-script form as represented in Shuowen style
items.caption: This modern rendering shows 荼 in the seal-script style associated with the Shuowen account. That account analyzes 荼 as 艸 with 余 as its phonetic element; it does not establish that every stroke of the later 茶 carried a separate meaning.
items.alt: Black seal-script form of 荼, with branching strokes above a central structure and long descending strokes below, on a white background.
items.selection_reason: The image is legible and identified as 荼 in Shuowen seal-script style. It helps illustrate the earlier graph relevant to 茶’s graphic history, while the account connects 荼 to 茶 without precisely dating the transition.
items.rights: Public domain, as stated on the Commons file page for this SVG representation.

limitations.text: This is a modern vector rendering, not an ancient artifact image. It illustrates a seal-script form of 荼 but cannot establish when the form was written or when 茶 became a distinct graph.
